headline: The audit purge anchor is signed — three statements could erase an audit trail and leave the chain verifying clean
summary:
The purge anchor is the one thing in the audit chain that says rows are ALLOWED to be missing. Every other tamper check compares a stored hash against a recomputed one, so deleting rows leaves a gap that verification catches; the anchor closes that gap by declaration. It was accepted on shape alone — 128 hex characters and a whole number — which is exactly what an attacker with write access supplies. Delete the rows, delete the checkpoints covering them, insert an anchor naming any hash and counter, and `b.audit.verify` reported a clean chain. That is fewer steps than the relink-and-forge attack the chain already refuses, and it erases more.

The anchor now carries a post-quantum signature over every field a reader acts on, and every place that reads it verifies it first: the chain walk, the contiguity guard on the next purge, the predecessor lookup that grounds the next archive's proof, and the append path itself, which needs the boundary to know where a purged chain resumes.

Upgrading with an existing purge anchor requires one boot with `acceptUnsignedPurgeAnchor: true`; see Migration.

items.title: A purge anchor must prove it was written with the audit-signing key (#674)
items.body:
`b.auditChain.verifyChain` adopted `lastPurgedRowHash` as the chain origin and skipped every row at or below `lastPurgedCounter` after checking only that the hash was 128 hex characters and the counter was a whole number. Both are trivially satisfiable by anyone who can write to the database, and the result was a verification that reported success over an arbitrary quantity of deleted history.

The anchor now carries `signature` and `publicKeyFingerprint`, signed by `b.auditSign` over the scope, boundary counter, boundary row hash, archive identifier and purge time. The signed layout is newline-delimited and refuses a newline inside any string field at both sign and verify time, so one signature can never verify two different readings of the same bytes. A boundary counter beyond `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` is refused for the same reason: the column is a BIGINT and the signed bytes carry the counter as text, so above that range two distinct stored values render identically and one signature would cover both. The same bound now applies wherever a counter is rendered into bytes that get signed — the consumer chain anchors in `b.auditSign` and the origin a `b.chainWriter` resumes from — through one shared predicate rather than three spellings of it. Its format string is distinct from the checkpoint and consumer-anchor formats, so a signature minted for one can never be replayed as another.

`b.auditChain.verifyPurgeAnchor` reports a status rather than a boolean, because the ways an anchor can fail to verify call for different reactions: `unsigned`, `forged`, `corrupt`, and `unchecked` — the last meaning the process holds no signing key and could not perform the check at all. Collapsing `unchecked` into `forged` would raise a tamper alarm on a healthy volume every time an offline verifier ran, and collapsing it into success would accept anything.

A clean result over a purge now says what was established and what was not: the boundary counter, whether the signature verified, the archive the anchor names, and whether anything actually found it. A signature proves this framework wrote the boundary; it says nothing about whether the archive still exists or holds those rows, and a report that ran the two together would be the wrong thing to hand an auditor.

Only the consumer knows where bundles are kept, so the check is theirs to supply: `b.auditChain.verifyChain(..., { resolveArchive })`, `b.db.init({ resolvePurgeArchive })` for the boot verify, and `blamejs audit verify-chain --archive-dir` for an offline one. With it, a boundary whose archive cannot be produced fails the verify instead of licensing the gap. Both resolvers are refused at the point they are supplied when they are present but not callable: they are consulted only when callable, so a typo or a config that failed to load would remove the very check that was asked for and return a clean result — a gap nothing can ever show the contents of. Without it the walk proceeds and the result says the archive was not resolved.

items.title: The next purge verifies the anchor it is about to extend
items.body:
Checking the anchor only at read time would have left it forgeable through the writer. An unsigned anchor carrying the real predecessor hash, followed by a legitimate purge of the next archive, would have had that purge sign the enlarged boundary — laundering the earlier deletion permanently, under a valid signature.

`b.auditTools.purge` verifies the existing anchor before extending it, and `b.auditTools.exportSlice` verifies it before using its hash to ground the next archive's chain proof. The signature is also computed before the rows are deleted rather than after: signing afterwards means an unavailable key leaves the rows already gone and an unsigned anchor over an unrecoverable deletion, which is the state a reader is now required to refuse. Failing before the delete costs nothing — the archive is on disk and the purge can be re-run.

items.title: A purge is a single-writer operation, start to finish
items.body:
Reading the anchor, deciding the new boundary is contiguous with it, and writing that boundary are one decision. Split across two steps they were two, and two overlapping purges could each find themselves contiguous with the same anchor and each overwrite the other's boundary — leaving rows deleted with nothing accounting for them, which verification then reports as clean, because the anchor is what licenses absence.

The whole sequence now runs under the audit chain's append lock, so an append cannot land between the deletion and the anchor that explains it either. `b.auditTools.purge` and `b.auditTools.signExistingPurgeAnchor` additionally require cluster leadership, which is what appends already require.

Leadership is not enough on its own, so the anchor also carries a fencing token. A superseded leader still holds a working handle, and during a handoff two nodes can both believe they hold it — no agreement between processes can settle that, only what is already stored. A purge reads the token before deleting anything and refuses outright if it has been passed, and the anchor write is refused by the database on the same test.

The boundary itself is fenced too, and separately from the token, because a boundary may only ever advance. A leader holding a HIGHER token can still be proposing a smaller range legitimately, and allowing that while another node was midway through deleting a larger one would leave rows above the surviving boundary gone with nothing accounting for them — the one state the anchor exists to make impossible. Held by the database, so no ordering between the two nodes has to be reasoned about.

`b.clusterStorage.fencedUpsert` is that operation, shared with the audit tip, which had the only implementation of it: MySQL can neither express the condition nor report the refusal, so it needs a read-back the other dialects do not, and one copy of that is enough.

items.title: A cluster purge can actually delete the rows it archived
items.body:
`b.frameworkSchema.ensureSchema` installs an append-only BEFORE-DELETE trigger on `audit_log` and `audit_checkpoints` for every dialect — that trigger is why a privileged actor cannot quietly remove an audit row. The cluster branch of the purge deleted straight through it, on the stated assumption that external databases had no such triggers, so a purge against Postgres or MySQL was refused by the guard every time.

With the boundary now recorded before the deletion, that refusal would leave the anchor advanced over rows still present, which verification then skips.

On Postgres the guard is never taken off and never switched off. It decides per row, permitting a DELETE only for a row at or below the boundary the purge anchor records — and the anchor is written before the rows go, so the guard allows exactly what the purge will remove and refuses everything else. Nothing is granted, which matters: a session setting is not an authorization, because `SET LOCAL` is available to any session holding the framework's own role, so a guard that honoured one could be self-granted by exactly the caller it exists to stop. What the guard does not do is worth stating, because the shape invites the opposite assumption: it does not stop a role that can UPDATE the anchor table, which can raise the boundary, delete what widening permits, and restore the signed row before committing. No rule expressible in a trigger closes that, because the same role supplies the input the rule reads. Making it authoritative against the application's own role needs an authorization that role cannot assume — a separate database role owning these tables and granting no UPDATE on the anchor, or append-only storage underneath — which is a deployment decision the schema cannot make for you. The guard covers the rest: an accidental DELETE from application code, and any role holding DML on the audit tables but not on the anchor. The detection that does not depend on privileges is the chain itself, where removing rows above the boundary breaks the hash linkage and removing the newest ones is what the tip sidecar's rollback check catches. **Installing the guard on MySQL needs a privilege worth checking before you upgrade.** With binary logging enabled — the default — MySQL refuses `CREATE TRIGGER` from a role without `SUPER`, and the `TRIGGER` privilege alone is not sufficient (measured on 8.4, where adding `SET_ANY_DEFINER` does not help either). Grant `SUPER` to the role the framework connects as, or set `log_bin_trust_function_creators=1` on the server. Boot now fails with an error naming both, instead of passing MySQL's own message through — a message that mentions neither the audit guard being installed nor the privilege that is missing. It is a failure rather than a warning on purpose: a volume reported as append-only with no guard on it is the worse outcome. MySQL and SQLite carry the same rule, so no dialect drops its guard for a purge any more. MySQL expresses the condition with `IF … THEN SIGNAL …; END IF`; the semicolon inside makes the body compound, which a protocol driver sends as one message — `DELIMITER` is a command-line construct, and the guard had been shaped around a test harness that needed it. SQLite carries the condition in a `WHEN` clause. Both, and Postgres, wrap the comparison in `COALESCE(..., FALSE)`: with no anchor row the comparison is NULL, and a guard that read that as no-restriction would leave the volume that has never authorized a deletion the least protected one.

That closes a window the previous approach left open — while a purge ran, any other connection holding the framework role could delete audit rows too, and a process killed mid-purge left the guard off until the next boot. The guard now stays installed throughout, on every dialect, including `consent_log`'s and every UPDATE guard, which no purge has any reason to touch.

Behind that trigger sat a second defect the deletion had never reached: it built its SQL without the active dialect, so on MySQL the boundary column was double-quoted and read as a string literal — the comparison failed with a truncated-value error rather than deleting anything. Both are fixed, and a cluster purge is now exercised end to end against live Postgres and MySQL rather than through an injected no-op.

items.title: An interrupted purge can be finished by re-running it
items.body:
The boundary is recorded before the rows it covers are deleted, because the two writes cannot be one transaction and the other order fails worse: a fence refused after the deletion would leave rows gone with nothing accounting for them, which no later purge can repair. Recording first means a refusal deletes nothing.

If the deletion then fails, the boundary describes rows that are still present, and verification skips them. Re-running the same archive now completes that deletion instead of being turned away as non-contiguous — read literally it is non-contiguous, and refusing it would have made the only repair available the one thing the guard rejected. Replaying an archive whose range the anchor already names deletes rows that are already gone, so nothing is gained by replaying one either.

"The same archive" means the whole range, not just where it ended. The anchor records `firstPurgedCounter` alongside the boundary and signs it, so an archive that ends at the same counter but starts later is a different, smaller archive and is refused. Without that, such a bundle would have passed as a retry, deleted everything through the boundary, and left the rows before its own start with no retained copy anywhere.

An anchor written before that field was covered still verifies: when the stored range start is `0` — the only value such an anchor can hold, and one that means the same thing in both layouts — verification retries against the shorter signed bytes. Such an anchor is held to the boundary alone when a retry is judged, too: chain counters begin at 1, so a stored `0` records no start rather than claiming one, and requiring it to equal the archive's start would turn away the very bundle that could finish an interrupted purge there — the contiguity check refuses it as well, since the anchor already ends where that archive ends. An anchor claiming a non-zero start gets no second chance, so this cannot be used to drop the field from an anchor that has one, and producing either signature still requires the signing key.

items.title: An audit write stops when the anchor cannot be believed
items.body:
Boot has always refused to start on an audit chain it cannot verify. The same now applies to tampering that happens while the process is running: if the purge anchor is present and does not verify, `b.audit.record` throws `audit/purge-anchor-not-verified` rather than starting a fresh chain.

Starting over looks like the cautious choice and is the opposite. The new rows would link to `ZERO_HASH` and, on a table a purge had emptied, take counters at or below the boundary the anchor claims — the range `verifyChain` skips. Every write between the tampering and the next verification would land there, linked to nothing and invisible to the check meant to catch it. Refusing costs an audit row; the alternative costs the chain its meaning.

items.title: A chain that resumes after a purge keeps its counters
items.body:
`b.audit.record` derived the next `monotonicCounter` from `MAX(monotonicCounter)`, which an emptied table answers with nothing. After a purge that removed every row, the next process restart therefore restarted the counter at 1 — at or below the purge boundary, which is exactly the range `verifyChain` skips. The rows were written, linked correctly to each other, and excluded from every verification that ever ran over them, with nothing reporting it.

The counter now resumes above the recorded boundary, alongside the hash. Both come from the same verified anchor, read once and cached, so neither can be restored without the other. In a cluster that cache also expires when leadership moves: a purge runs on one node, and a node that led before it and leads again after it would otherwise still hold the pre-purge answer and link its next row to nothing — turning a legitimate purge into a reported chain break. The fencing token is what crosses nodes, so an origin read under an earlier term is re-read rather than trusted. The read itself is a database round trip, so the term is checked again once it returns: an origin fetched just before another node purged describes a chain that no longer exists, and noticing on the next append would be too late for the row this one is about to write. Leadership that will not settle refuses the append instead of linking to a boundary that may already be superseded and an append does not pay for a database read per row.

A purge discards that cached answer before it releases the chain lock. A counter primed while the purge was midway through — after the rows were deleted, before the anchor accounting for them was written — would otherwise have survived as 1 for the life of the process.

items.title: A mail TLS pair that will not load says which file is wrong (#672)
items.body:
`b.mail.server.tls.context` refused a bad certificate pair with OpenSSL's own text and named neither file — `error:05800074:x509 certificate routines::key values mismatch` and nothing else. Those are the two commonest operator mistakes with a TLS pair, both arrive at boot with the server refusing to start, and in both cases the next question is which file: a host mid-renewal has several candidates and usually a symlink, and this function is the only thing that knows which pair it just compared.

The refusal now leads with what is wrong in words, lists the certificate and key paths, and keeps the OpenSSL string after them rather than instead of them. Paths only — a key supplied as a vault-sealed blob is named by its path, never by anything it unsealed to.

**An empty or truncated file is now refused at startup instead of accepted.** This came out of testing the above and is the more serious half. `createSecureContext` does not object to a missing certificate — a context without one is what a TLS *client* uses, and is perfectly legal — so a mail server handed an empty `certFile` started cleanly, advertised STARTTLS, and failed every handshake at runtime. An interrupted renewal leaves exactly that file, and the failure surfaced as far as it is possible to get from its cause. A file holding no PEM block is refused by name.

Where the framework knows which file is at fault it names that one; naming both is reserved for the mismatch, where each file is individually fine and only the pair is wrong.

items.title: A failed open no longer leaves the decrypted database behind (#678)
items.body:
Under `atRest: "encrypted"` the live database is a decrypted working copy in `tmpDir`, and `removePlaintextFiles()` is what stops it outliving the process that made it. An open that threw AFTER claiming that copy never reached it: `close()` returned immediately when `initialized` was false, and that flag says only that init did not FINISH — nothing about what it had already taken. So a failed open left plaintext exactly where the design says none persists, in the case nobody is watching, because the caller saw a throw and moved on.

The claim is now tracked in its own right. `close()` releases it, and `b.db.init` releases it itself when it throws, so recovery does not depend on the caller remembering a `close()` in a `catch`. It is deliberately NOT keyed on the working-copy path alone: that path survives a previous open in the same process, and cleaning up on it would delete a different database's copy when an open failed before claiming anything.

Removing the files also closes the database handle first. Windows refuses to unlink a file another handle holds open, and those unlinks swallow their errors — so on a path that never closed the handle, the ownership record beside the copy disappeared while the decrypted database stayed, which in a directory listing reads exactly like a cleanup that worked.

The stale sweep can also see what it leaves. It enumerated names ending in `.db`, and the ownership record is `<name>.db.owner` — so a record whose working copy was gone was invisible to it permanently, one more every time an open failed, in the directory that holds decrypted databases. It now enumerates on the prefix and considers both names as one volume. A record whose owner is still running is left alone, because the claim is written BEFORE the copy exists and that is what a peer mid-open looks like; one whose owner is gone, or that is too damaged to name an owner at all, is reclaimed. That last case is a deliberate departure from the rule governing an actual database, where anything unprovable is left alone: removing a database costs data, while a record accounting for nothing costs only the pile it builds.

items.title: A read-only open no longer tries to migrate the volume it is inspecting
items.body:
`b.db.init({ readOnly: true })` ran the declarative schema reconcile like any other open. That is a no-op only when the live schema already matches the declaration — and a volume written by an earlier version does not match, because it is missing whatever columns that version had not declared yet. Reconcile answered the difference with `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN`, the handle refused the write, and the open failed.

So the flag whose purpose is inspecting a database without touching it worked on every volume except the older ones an inspection is most likely to be about — and this release, which adds two columns to the purge-anchor table, would have made that the common case. A read-only open now takes the schema as it finds it. Every framework read of a possibly-older table already tolerates the columns being absent.

items.title: Framework DDL quotes its table name, matching every read of it
items.body:
`b.frameworkSchema.setTablePrefix` accepts any valid SQL identifier, and the generated `CREATE TABLE` / `CREATE INDEX` / trigger statements interpolated the resulting name unquoted while `b.sql` quotes identifiers when it builds the queries that read those tables. On Postgres an unquoted identifier folds to lower case, so a mixed-case prefix created `_Blamejs_audit_log` as `_blamejs_audit_log` and the quoted reads then looked for a table that was never there.

Both sides now quote. Under the default all-lowercase prefix the two forms address the identical table on every supported dialect, so nothing changes for a deployment that never set a custom prefix.

items.title: A purged chain resumes rather than restarting
items.body:
`b.chainWriter.create` accepts `resolveOrigin`, which the table's owner uses to say where its chain continues when the table holds no rows for a key — `{ hash, counter }`, or nothing, in which case an empty table starts a new chain at `ZERO_HASH` from counter 1 as before. `b.audit` supplies one that reads the verified purge anchor.

`b.audit.withChainLock(fn)` runs `fn` holding the append lock, for a caller that has to change what the chain reads while nothing appends to it.

items.title: `b.time.monotonicMs` and `b.time.stopwatch` (#666)
items.body:
Measuring how long something took had no right answer on `b`. The nearest-looking one, `b.time.monotonicNow`, is not it: its guarantee is ORDERING — values that never repeat and never go backwards — and it is built over `Date.now()`, so an operator correcting the host forward carries that correction into the number, and subtracting two readings reports time that never passed. A consumer was left choosing between the wall clock and hand-rolling `process.hrtime.bigint()`.

`b.time.monotonicMs()` returns milliseconds from a source no clock correction can move. The value means nothing on its own — it counts from an arbitrary point, so it is not a timestamp and cannot be stored or compared across processes — but the difference between two readings is elapsed time. `b.time.stopwatch()` wraps that for the common case, returning a reader with `ms()` and `reset()`. Neither takes a source: a configurable one would let a caller point the steppable-proof primitive back at the wall clock, which is the mistake they exist to prevent.

Use them for anything whose correctness depends on how much time has passed rather than on what time it is — a lease, a rate window, a refill interval, a timeout. A forward correction on a wall-clock-measured lease reaps a lock a session is still holding; on a rate window it hands back the whole budget with no time having passed, so the documented ceiling stops being the ceiling kept.

The framework had four private copies of the conversion, in `metrics`, the request logger, `server-timing` and `stream-throttle`; they now share this one. Two of them carried a `Date.now()` fallback for environments without `hrtime` — unreachable on any supported Node, and the one path that could put a correctable clock behind a duration, including a negative one on a host stepped backwards mid-request. Those are gone with the local conversions.

`b.time.monotonicNow`'s documentation now says what it is not for, since its name is what a reader looking for elapsed time finds first.

items.title: `b.clusterStorage.fencedUpsert`
items.body:
Upsert a single row only if the caller's fencing token is at least the one already stored, and report whether it was refused. This is how a single-writer table stays single-writer across processes, and it is one primitive rather than a shape each caller re-derives because the three dialects disagree about it: Postgres and SQLite take a `WHERE` on the conflict clause and report the refusal by returning no rows, while MySQL's `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE` has neither and its fence becomes a per-column `IF()` that changes nothing while still succeeding. Detection there has to read the token back afterwards.

`fenceColumns` names several columns that must ALL be non-decreasing, for a value that may only ever advance — a boundary, a high-water mark. Holding that in the database rather than in whoever writes next is the difference between an invariant and a convention, and a writer with the right token can still be proposing the wrong direction.

items.title: `b.auditSign.pinnedKeyResolver`, `b.auditSign.canonicalPublicKeyPem` and `b.auditSign.publicKeyLicensingDeletion`
items.body:
Three small primitives for naming a key, extracted because the same rule was being restated at each place a key is supplied and drifting between them.

`canonicalPublicKeyPem(pem)` re-exports a key through the parsed form, giving one spelling for one key. `pinnedKeyResolver(pem)` builds a `resolvePublicKey` for a single operator-supplied key that answers for either fingerprint that key can legitimately carry — the text as supplied and the re-export — and nothing else; `blamejs audit verify-chain --public-key` and `db.init({ purgeAnchorPublicKey })` both route through it, so a key saved with different line endings resolves the same either way. `publicKeyLicensingDeletion(fingerprint)` answers for the live signing key alone, which is what a purge anchor is verified against.

items.title: `b.auditChain.verifyPurgeAnchor` and `b.auditChain.purgeAnchorPayload`
items.body: The verification a caller needs when reading an audit database it did not open through `b.db.init` — a forensic check, a restore validation, a downstream auditor. `verifyPurgeAnchor(row, { resolvePublicKey })` takes the key from the caller when the process has none of its own; `purgeAnchorPayload(anchor)` builds the canonical signed bytes.

items.title: `blamejs audit verify-chain --public-key` and `--archive-dir`
items.body:
The command opens a database file directly and never initializes signing, so it holds no key with which to check the anchor that licenses any deleted rows. Point `--public-key` at the audit-signing public key and the anchor is verified; without it, a purged chain now exits 3 (`UNCHECKED`) rather than claiming a verification it did not perform. The key is parsed and re-exported before its fingerprint is taken, so the same key saved with different line endings is still the same key. `audit-sign.pubkeys.json` records keys rotated out, so an anchor signed before a rotation can still be resolved from the PEM it holds. That file is unsealed, which is what lets a verifier read it with no passphrase — so an entry now has to hash to the fingerprint it is filed under. Without that check, anyone able to write the file could file their own key under an expected fingerprint, sign a boundary with the matching private key, and have verification accept it, never touching the wrapped key. Both lookups over that file run the same check. Making an entry hash to its own label stops one key being filed under another's name, but it cannot make an unsealed file AUTHORITATIVE — generating a keypair and adding a self-consistent entry for it needs no secret — so a rotated-out key no longer licenses deleted rows at all. Only the live key does, and it lives sealed behind a passphrase the process had to be given. A checkpoint signed before a rotation still verifies from the history, because attesting that a tip existed only adds a claim; a purge anchor erases, which is a different weight. **Rotating the audit-signing key on a volume that has purged now needs one more step:** call `b.auditTools.signExistingPurgeAnchor()` afterwards to re-sign the anchor under the new key. Until then the chain refuses to verify and says so, naming that call. Rotating and re-signing are two calls, so a process can exit between them and leave a volume whose anchor names the outgoing key — and the repair needs a booted database, which is what the refused anchor prevents. `db.init({ acceptRotatedPurgeAnchorKey: true })` is the way back in: one boot, it re-signs under the live key and then does nothing. It stays a flag rather than an automatic fixup because the evidence that the anchor verifies under the old key comes from the unsealed history, and re-signing on that alone would launder a planted key into the live one. The flag is the operator saying they performed the rotation. The same reasoning removed a fallback under `auditSigning: false`: with no key loaded, boot used to resolve the anchor's key from that unsealed history, which is the attacker vouching for themselves one configuration over. It no longer does — the anchor reports as unchecked, which that posture already permits, so the volume opens and nothing claims a proof it did not make. An operator who wants it genuinely verified there passes `db.init({ purgeAnchorPublicKey })`, a trust root they chose, still bound to the fingerprint the anchor names. It reports the anchor as naming a rotated-out key rather than as a forgery, because it is not one, and the re-sign checks the existing signature under that rotated key first so a tampered anchor cannot be laundered into a valid one, and `b.auditChain.verifyChain` repeats it at the point of use: the key a purge anchor is verified under must hash to the fingerprint the anchor names. `resolvePublicKey` is an extension point, so without that the binding would hold only as far as each resolver was careful, and one returning a key the anchor does not name yields a signature that verifies perfectly against the wrong key. A key is also matched on the text it was stored as WELL as on a re-export: `rotateSigningKey` records an operator-supplied key exactly as written, so one saved with CRLF line endings was fingerprinted that way, and hashing only a re-export would report those volumes as signed by an unknown key. Supplied keys are canonicalized when they are ingested now, so one key has one spelling from here on.

`--archive-dir` says where archive bundles live. With it, an anchor naming an archive that is not there fails the verify; without it, the result names the archive and states plainly that nothing resolved it. Bundles are matched by the identifier inside their own manifest, together with the range the anchor signed, rather than by directory name, which the operator chooses, and a bundle whose encrypted rows are missing does not count as found, nor does one missing the covering checkpoint an archive cannot be read back without, nor one whose payload no longer hashes to the digest **the anchor signed for it**. That digest is the load-bearing part: a manifest states its own checksums and travels with the bytes it describes, so an attacker who replaces `rows.enc` replaces the checksum beside it and the two still agree — comparing them shows only that the bundle is consistent with itself. The anchor records the digest of the archive the purge actually verified, inside the signed payload, so which bytes the archive has to be is a claim only the signing key can make. A replacement that is internally perfect is refused — present is not the same as intact, and a blob altered in place decrypts to nothing. The range matters because the identifier is the covering checkpoint's, and one checkpoint can cover several archived slices: on the identifier alone, a surviving sibling would answer for the slice that went missing — a manifest naming the right archive is not the archive.

The result also says which range that archive covers. Each purge replaces the anchor, so after several contiguous ones the boundary licenses everything below it while the row names only the newest bundle; letting one resolved archive stand for the whole licensed range would claim a recoverability nothing checked.

items.title: Additive column migration for framework tables
items.body:
`b.frameworkSchema.ensureSchema` issues `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN` for columns declared on a table that already exists. `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` is a no-op against a table that is already there, so before this a column added to a framework table reached only fresh deployments and the first write naming it failed everywhere else.

The ALTER is generated from the same column declaration the CREATE is built from, so the two cannot disagree, and a column that is NOT NULL without a DEFAULT is refused at build time rather than failing against live data — no engine can fill one for rows that already exist.

items.title: An installation that has already purged needs one boot with `acceptUnsignedPurgeAnchor: true`
items.body:
A purge performed by 0.18.57 or earlier left an anchor with no signature, which this release refuses. Re-running the purge does not produce a signed one: the contiguity guard requires an archive starting one counter past the recorded boundary, and the boundary is what is in question.

So boot once with `b.db.init({ acceptUnsignedPurgeAnchor: true })`. That signs the anchor in place, pinning the boundary it already claims so it can never be moved again, and logs what it pinned. Then remove the flag — it does nothing afterwards, and a second run reports that the anchor is already signed rather than rewriting it.

This pins the boundary rather than proving it. Nothing can distinguish a boundary an earlier version wrote from one somebody else did, which is why the signature exists; an operator who needs the boundary proven verifies the retained archive against the chain with `b.auditTools.verifyBundle` before running it. `b.auditTools.signExistingPurgeAnchor()` is the operation itself, callable directly. It refuses a corrupt or already-forged anchor rather than pinning it — that would turn a detectable problem into a permanent one.

A deployment running `b.db.init({ auditSigning: false })` is unaffected. It has no key to sign with, so it writes unsigned anchors and accepts them; the writer allows exactly what the verifier allows.

Deployments that have never purged have no anchor and need nothing.
